tracks.title: The kind problem
tracks.text: Lesson 04 point 7 — tags. A deep-dive under org, the written layer. [curious] Here's the problem hiding in plain sight. You've already met headlines and TODO states. But everything in your tree is the same kind of thing. A heading is a heading. So how does a machine know which heading is a toolkit it should hand to an agent… which subtree should compile and run… which heading is an agent's own identity… and which is just a note to yourself? The usual answers all bolt a second system onto the document. Filenames. Magic directories. A little typed header in a different grammar. Or a registry — an index file that drifts out of sync the first time someone edits the real thing without updating the list. Every one of those is a second place where truth lives. And the document and the list… eventually disagree. The question worth asking — could the kind annotation live inside the grammar itself? So there's nothing to keep in sync, because there's only one thing.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A tag is a word in the trailing colon-run of an org headline — the kind annotation machines filter on. It's stripped from the title, never shown as text, and carried in every query row. [curious] One tag turns a heading into a role the runtime reacts to. Org's own thesis says it, right at the top of the one parser everything shares — org is a language, not just syntax. TODO state… tags… drawers… source blocks — all carry meaning. So the trailing tag isn't decoration the way a hashtag is. It's the type annotation of the written layer. And the kernel treats it as load-bearing.

tracks.title: How a tag is read
tracks.text: How a tag is read. The mechanics are small and exact — and that's the point. Picture a real workflow file. Line one… a heading, Nightly digest, and way out at the right margin, colon workflow colon. Below it, three children — Fetch events… Summarize… Send — each ending in colon component colon. Four facts govern how the kernel reads those. First — trailing run only. The tag is the last token that starts and ends with a colon. A colon in the middle of a title is just a colon. Second — colon a colon b colon is two tags. The kernel extracts a flat list. Colon workflow colon gives you one entry. Colon a colon b colon gives you two. Third — stripped from the title. The kernel removes that trailing run, so the title comes back clean — Nightly digest — not Nightly digest with the tag dangling off it. A tag is metadata, not title text. Fourth — exact string match. The whole tag check is one question — does this heading's tag list contain that exact string. No globbing… no hierarchy… no case folding. Capital-W Workflow is not workflow. That's the entire reading model. Three lines of Rust do the matching. Everything downstream is built on that one check.

tracks.title: The five tags that run the ecosystem
tracks.text: Now the heart of the page — the five tags that run the ecosystem. [excited] Most tags you'll ever write are inert labels the runtime ignores. And that's fine. But five tags are canon — each one is read by a specific module, and carrying it turns a heading into something the system acts on. Let me walk them, one tag, one role. First — colon workflow colon. The Workflow module reacts, and the heading becomes a DAG — its component children are the tasks, its header args are the edges. Second — colon component colon. The kernel's build-plan reacts, and the heading becomes a task leaf — a unit of code inside a world. Third — colon toolkit colon. The Toolkits module reacts, and the heading becomes a discoverable capability, found by a tag query. Fourth — colon agent colon. The AgentDef module reacts, and the heading becomes a runnable identity — it reads an ID, a model, and a toolkit list off the same heading. And fifth — colon member colon. The Workspace module reacts, and the heading becomes a workspace entry — a participant carrying a decentralized ID and a path. Read all five as one sentence repeated. A word at the end of a heading hands that heading to exactly one part of the runtime… which treats it as exactly one kind of thing. Nothing else about the heading changed. Same indentation, same prose, same drawers. As the workflow module puts it — a native org workflow headline IS the DAG. No DSL. No board model. The tag is the whole declaration.

tracks.title: Tags on the query surface
tracks.text: Tags on the query surface. Because every headline row carries its tags, the document is queryable by kind — with no extra index. Run the real verb against the real file — wbx query, nightly-digest dot org. Back comes a row. Level one… title, Nightly digest… tags, a list containing just workflow… a schedule for six a.m. daily… and empty everywhere else. Two things to notice in that row. The title came back without the tag — the strip already happened. And tags is a list — a two-tag run would show two entries. So filtering by kind is just filtering rows. From the shell, give me every task in this workflow is one line — pipe the query into jq, select the rows whose tags include component, print the titles. Out come three — Fetch events… Summarize… Send. The runtime does the very same thing in Elixir, and this is the part worth sitting with. The entire toolkit-discovery subsystem is one filter over those same rows. No registry. No index file. Discovery IS a tag query — parse the headlines, keep the ones where toolkit is in the tag list, return them. The real heading it finds is ffmpeg, multimedia processing, colon toolkit colon — registered by nothing but the word at the end of its title. Picture the whole pipeline as a fork in a river. One org file flows into parse-headlines, which emits one row per heading, each carrying its tags. Then the river splits three ways by a single test. Rows whose tags include toolkit flow to discoverable toolkits. Rows tagged agent flow to runnable identities. Rows tagged workflow flow to compilable worlds. One file in… three kinds of thing out… [excited] and the only thing doing the sorting is a word. One honest note on syntax. The docs sketch a fuller query language — composable expressions like, and, tags toolkit, property ID wb. That parser is not shipped as a kernel export today. What ships is what you just heard — query returns all the rows, and the tag filter lives one step later, in jq at the shell or one line of Elixir in the host.

tracks.title: The tag that compiles
tracks.text: Next — and this one's a depth rung, skippable — the tag that compiles. Discovery is filtering. Compilation is the strongest form of a tag doing something. The kernel's build-plan walks the tree, and a tag decides what each heading is allowed to become. A top-level heading is only treated as a world if it's tagged workflow. Inside a world, each descendant is asked its tag — tagged workflow, recurse into a sub-world… tagged component, become a task leaf with code. And validate skips — literally steps past — any heading not tagged workflow. Untagged headings are invisible to the compiler. Picture the tree. At the top, Nightly digest, colon workflow colon — build-plan opens a world. Hanging off it, three children, each colon component colon — Fetch events becomes a Rust task, Summarize a JavaScript task, Send a Go task. They're wired in a chain — Fetch's output flows into Summarize's input, Summarize's output into Send's. And then a fourth child — Notes, with no tag at all — sits right there in the same tree, and the compiler never looks at it. Out the bottom drops the world JSON — one world, three tasks, the plan the engine runs. The tree never gained a build file or a config block. One tag on the parent, one on each child — [chuckles] that was the entire build specification.

tracks.title: Tags, states, and properties
tracks.text: Now — tags, states, and properties. A tag carries kind. And only kind. It's tempting to reach for a tag whenever you want to annotate a heading, but the written layer divides that labor across four carriers, and keeping them apart is what keeps the grammar legible. Four questions, four mechanisms. What kind is this — answered by a tag — colon workflow colon, colon component colon. What state is it in — answered by a TODO keyword — TODO, DOING, DONE. What data does it hold — answered by a property in a drawer — like ID ffmpeg. And what does it mean — answered by the body and the header args, the prose and the output-to-input edges. The verdict you can carry everywhere — reach for a tag only when you're naming a kind. State is a TODO keyword. A heading moves from TODO to DOING to DONE without its tag ever changing. Data is a property. Meaning is the body. And the proof the system holds this line is a deliberate counter-example. The native TODO outline runs with — in its own words — no custom tags, nothing an agent has to learn. A plain outline with states, nesting, and a couple of ordered-and-blocker properties does the whole job. The ecosystem reaches for tags to mark kind… never for state, never for data — because it already has the right tool for each.

tracks.title: A tag is not a permission
tracks.text: A tag is not a permission. This one is easy to get wrong, so let me be sharp about it. A toolkit tag makes a heading discoverable. It does not make it trusted. And it does not make it runnable. The toolkits module says it bluntly — a toolkit dropped there is untrusted supply-chain input. Discovery is one query. Trust is a separate gate. The discovery root is unauthenticated — anyone can drop a manifest with a toolkit tag on it and it will show up in a query. That's by design — discovery and trust are different concerns. Execution is gated separately, downstream, by an explicit capability grant — the same grants-not-inheritance posture the rest of the architecture runs on. So a tag is a label that makes something findable… never a key that makes something allowed. [sarcastic] Mixing those two up is the classic supply-chain mistake. The written layer keeps them apart, on purpose.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: [curious] Now the honest part — where it bites. The tag model is deliberately small, and the smallness has edges. First — flat strings, exact match only. No globbing, no case folding. Capital-T Toolkit and lowercase toolkit are different tags, and nothing warns you. Second — no inheritance. Emacs org-mode pushes a parent's tags down to its children. This kernel does not. The check looks only at a heading's own list. Tag the parent workflow and the children are not automatically anything — they each need their own component tag. Third — no special org conventions. Org-mode's noexport and archive behaviors are simply not implemented — grep the runtime and you get zero hits. A tag named noexport is just another inert label here. Fourth — and this is the one that bites hardest — misspelling is silent invisibility. Write Nightly digest, colon w-o-r-k-f-l-w colon — a typo — and the compiler does not error. Build-plan ignores the heading because it isn't tagged workflow. Validate reports nothing because there's nothing tagged workflow to check. The plan doesn't fail… it vanishes. Hear the difference. Run wbx tangle on the good file, tagged workflow — out comes worlds, with three tasks inside. Run it on the same file with the typo — out comes worlds, empty. No error. No diagnostics. Just gone. [sighs] With tags, the failure mode is never a stack trace. It's an empty result. The tree looks fine, the file parses, and the thing you meant to declare simply isn't there — because the machine read the string you actually wrote, not the one you meant. And last — that composable query language, the s-expression syntax, is direction, not shipped. Today, you filter rows.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I invent my own tags? Yes — freely. Unknown tags are inert labels. The runtime parses them and carries them in every query row, but only the canon five switch machinery on. Tag a heading urgent or draft and it's a label you can filter on yourself with jq — it just won't compile or get discovered. Useful, harmless, yours. Why a tag and not a property? Because they answer different questions. A tag is the heading's kind — cheap to scan, one membership check, and it's what the runtime branches on. A property is data the heading carries. You tag a heading agent to say it IS an agent. You give it an ID property to say WHICH agent. Kind, then detail. Do child headings inherit my tag? No — unlike Emacs. Nothing propagates downward. If you want a child to be a component, tag the child. And — my workflow silently does nothing, why? First suspect — a misspelled tag. The compiler only opens a world for a heading tagged exactly workflow, and only treats a child as a task if it's tagged exactly component. A typo produces no error and no diagnostics — just an empty plan. Run wbx query and read the tags field on each row. [chuckles] What the kernel sees is what's actually there — not what you meant.

tracks.title: Back up to org
tracks.text: So that's tags. A word at the end of a heading… that hands that heading to one part of the runtime as one kind of thing. Colon workflow colon compiles. Colon toolkit colon is discovered. Colon agent colon runs. No registry anywhere — discovery is parse, then filter. The tag IS the registry. And it carries kind, and only kind — state lives in the TODO keyword, data lives in a drawer. The way back up is short. This is a deep-dive under org — lesson four — the written layer where tags, states, drawers, and source blocks all carry meaning. Go back there for the whole grammar. And one last thing — view source on this page. [mischievously] There's a comment in it that is valid org, with a three-tag run. The same kernel that compiles every workbook would read it as structure, not prose. [chuckles] The format eats itself. That's the written layer.
